stories.title: Work Underway on 17-Story McKinney Office Building
stories.excerpt: Stonelake Capital Partners broke ground on 2626 McKinney, its new 17-story office building on McKinney Avenue. The Dallas Business Journal reports the tower will have 173,774 square feet of office space along with 7,067 square feet of ground-floor retail space in Uptown. Stonelake announced in June that it secured construction financing for the tower from Bank OZK. It’s located next to Whole Foods grocery store and a short walk from The Crescent, The Ritz-Carlton, S&D Oyster Bar and other popular restaurants, shops and amenities. Stonelake bought the Uptown site in 2021. The building will feature an 11th-floor amenity level with a terrace overlooking the Dallas skyline. Brasfield & Gorrie will serve as the general contractor. 2626 McKinney will be delivered in early 2028. The post Work Underway on 17-Story McKinney Office Building appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Stonelake Capital breaks ground on 173,774 SF office tower, McKinney Avenue Uptown Dallas.
Bank OZK financed; delivery early 2028; 11th-floor amenity level with skyline terrace.
Location next to Whole Foods, The Ritz-Carlton, restaurants signals strong urban anchoring.
stories.summary: Stonelake Capital Partners has begun construction on 2626 McKinney, a 17-story office building delivering 173,774 SF of Class A office and 7,067 SF of ground-floor retail in Uptown Dallas. The project, financed by Bank OZK, will complete in early 2028. The site sits in a high-amenity corridor anchored by Whole Foods, luxury hotels, and dining.
stories.impact: Office construction in Dallas's premium Uptown submarket does not directly drive multifamily demand, but signals continued urban density and corporate tenant confidence in the Dallas CBD. However, office-heavy development can absorb capital and construction labor, potentially increasing hard costs for concurrent residential projects and competing for skilled trades through 2028 delivery.

stories.title: Rexford Plans Up to $2B in Sales After Posting $507M Loss in Q2
stories.excerpt: Rexford Industrial Realty is dramatically accelerating its shift from being the most aggressive industrial buyer in Southern California into perhaps the region’s biggest seller. The Los Angeles-based real estate investment trust (REIT) has identified about $2 billion of “noncore assets” for disposition as it continues to prioritize keeping tenants in Rexford buildings. That property sales forecast is sharply up from the previous range of $400 million to $500 million. During the REIT’s earnings call Friday, CEO Laura Clark said the disposition pool encompasses about 8 million square feet with limited value-creation potential, shorter lease terms, and rents substantially above market — generally by more than 20 percent. Chief Financial Officer Michael Fitzmaurice said about $1 billion will repay debt maturing in 2027, rather than refinance into a higher rate environment. The remaining proceeds will be guided by market conditions. “We’re not de-levering to sit idle; we’re de-levering to redeploy,” Fitzmaurice said. The vast majority of Rexford’s property sales are expected to close before the end of the year. “We expect that pricing will be achieved at levels that allow us to redeploy proceeds on a neutral to accretive basis through our 2027 FFO per share, and this is not a dilutive exercise,” Clark said. Rexford said it sold seven properties totaling approximately 572,000 square feet for $137.9 million during the second quarter, after disposing of five properties for $127.4 million in the first quarter. The company previously known for 10-figure buying sprees has completed no acquisitions this year. Rexford plans to use property sales proceeds to repay debt, repurchase shares and pursue higher-yielding investments. It bought back $100 million of stock during the quarter, bringing its 2026 repurchases to $300 million, and its board subsequently authorized a new $1 billion repurchase program. The ramped-up disposition strategy also came with a $506.9 million
bullets: Rexford Industrial accelerates $2B asset sales vs. prior $400–500M guidance; 8M SF noncore pool.
CEO Laura Clark: rents 20%+ above market, shorter lease terms; $1B repay 2027 debt.
Strategy pivot from buyer to seller; proceeds to redeploy into higher-return assets.
stories.summary: Rexford Industrial Realty, the most aggressive Southern California industrial buyer, is sharply pivoting to seller mode. The REIT has identified ~$2 billion of noncore assets (8 million SF) with limited value creation, rents well above market (20%+), and shorter lease terms. About $1 billion will repay debt maturing in 2027 rather than refinance at higher rates; remaining proceeds will be redeployed strategically.
stories.impact: Rexford's liquidation of ~8M SF of overrented SoCal industrial assets signals the firm has reached peak acquisition risk and is de-risking ahead of a potential economic slowdown or further rate pressure. The $1B debt repayment strategy indicates REITs are prioritizing balance-sheet strength over growth; this constrains multifamily capital competition in Southern California as equity redeploys defensively, but also signals cap-rate floors may hold firm if distressed sales spike.

stories.title: Historic Downtown Denver Building Hits the Market
stories.excerpt: It’s probably best known as The George. It was called that for over 100 years. Now called The Symes Buildings, the nearly 100,000 square foot building is up for sale. The Denver Business Journal reports the totally vacant building at 820 16th St. was listed for sale as a bank-owned foreclosure and redevelopment opportunity. The sale is a traditional investment sale rather than an auction. The asking price for the 120-year-old building was not publicly available. Harbor Associates, which purchased the building for $17.2 million in 2022, defaulted on an $18.66 million loan from Thorofare Capital. Thorofare ultimately acquired the property for $6 million at a foreclosure auction in February. The property is being advertised as including an approved site plan valid until 2030. Future developers have zoning rights to convert the property to residential use. A buyer could pursue another use that reactivates the building. The post Historic Downtown Denver Building Hits the Market appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Historic 100,000 SF Denver building (120 years old) foreclosed; Thorofare Capital acquired for $6M.
Zoning permits residential conversion; approved site plan valid through 2030; bank-owned redevelopment opportunity.
Original purchaser Harbor Associates defaulted on $18.66M loan after 2022 $17.2M acquisition.
stories.summary: The Symes Building (formerly known as The George), a 120-year-old, nearly 100,000 SF structure at 820 16th St. in Downtown Denver, has been foreclosed and is now listed for sale by Thorofare Capital (which acquired it for $6 million at auction in February after Harbor Associates defaulted). The property carries approved zoning rights for residential conversion, with the site plan valid through 2030.
stories.impact: Downtown Denver's historic office-to-residential conversion pipeline now has a distressed asset with existing entitlements, lowering development risk and timeline for an opportunistic buyer. The 2022-to-2024 arc (acquisition crash) signals tight underwriting on adaptive reuse; the approved zoning is a major value unlock for a developer with capital and execution expertise in Denver's soft downtown market.

stories.title: NMHC Sees Declines in Capital Availability, Deal Flow in Latest Survey
stories.excerpt: Apartment market conditions tightened over the past three months, with conditions for debt and equity financing worsening while deal flow decreased, the National Multifamily Housing Council (NMHC) reported in its July Quarterly Survey of Apartment Market Conditions. However, rent growth and vacancies represented a bright spot. The Market Tightness Index (57) came in above the breakeven level of 50, indicating higher rent growth and lower vacancies. The Sales Volume Index (46) signaled a pullback in deal flow, while the Equity Financing Index (44) and the Debt Financing Index (46) reflected less availability of capital. “Job growth picked up somewhat during the first half of the year after a lackluster 2025,” said Chris Bruen, NMHC senior director of research and chief economist. “This, combined with declining apartment deliveries, helped translate to modestly tighter conditions—higher rent growth and lower vacancy rates—over the past three months.” He continued, “Even so, rents continued to decrease in many high-supply sunbelt markets. At the same time, higher inflation has led to higher interest rates, worsening borrowing conditions, and a corresponding pullback in equity capital.” The post NMHC Sees Declines in Capital Availability, Deal Flow in Latest Survey appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: NMHC Q3 survey: Market Tightness Index 57 (above 50 breakeven); Sales Volume Index 46 (pullback).
Equity Financing Index 44, Debt Financing Index 46 both signal capital contraction; declining deliveries supporting rents.
Job growth rebound, lower vacancies mask regional divergence; sunbelt markets see rent declines despite supply deceleration.
stories.summary: The National Multifamily Housing Council's July quarterly survey shows apartment markets tightening with higher rent growth and lower vacancy (Market Tightness Index: 57), but financing and deal flow contracting sharply (Sales Volume Index: 46; Equity Financing Index: 44; Debt Financing Index: 46). Declining deliveries and modest job growth rebound support rents, though sunbelt high-supply markets continue rent pressure despite supply declines.
stories.impact: Capital scarcity is the dominant signal: equity and debt financing indices in the 44–46 range indicate structured pullback by lenders and sponsors, narrowing acquisition windows and raising cost of capital for new development. Tighter markets (lower vacancies, higher rents) are concentrated in supply-constrained coastal/sun markets; high-delivery sunbelt metros will experience continued rent headwinds, pressuring underwriting and slowing starts in Austin, Phoenix, Charlotte until supply normalizes.

stories.title: Keller Inks $718.5M Refi on 13 SW USA Rental Communities
stories.excerpt: Keller Investment Properties will refinance a 13-property portfolio through a $718.5 million CMBS loan. Six are in Utah, four in Nevada and three in Arizona. Multihousing News reports that a Nomura affiliate will provide a two-year, floating-rate, interest-only loan. Approximately $696.3 million will refinance existing debt, while $22.2 million will cover closing costs and reserves. The collateral includes 12 multifamily communities and one student housing asset, totaling 3,321 units. The properties were completed between 1987 and 2022, with a weighted-average construction year of 2004. The collection’s weighted-average rent was $1,632 per unit. Midland Loan Services, a division of PNC Bank, will be the master servicer, while Argentic Services Co. will act as the special servicer. Computershare Trust Co. will be the trustee and certificate administrator. BellOak LLC will serve as the operating advisor. The post Keller Inks $718.5M Refi on 13 SW USA Rental Communities appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Keller Investment Properties refi $718.5M CMBS via Nomura; 13 properties (6 UT, 4 NV, 3 AZ).
3,321 units, weighted-average rent $1,632, construction 1987–2022; floating-rate, interest-only, 2-year term.
Approximate $696.3M refinances existing debt; Midland/PNC master servicer; strong multifamily CMBS market signal.
stories.summary: Keller Investment Properties has secured a $718.5 million CMBS refi via Nomura for 13 properties across Utah (6), Nevada (4), and Arizona (3), totaling 3,321 units with a weighted-average rent of $1,632. The floating-rate, interest-only, two-year loan refinances ~$696.3M in existing debt. Multifamily and one student housing asset, weighted-average construction year 2004.
stories.impact: Nomura's ability to price a large single-bank SASB CMBS for a well-seasoned Southwest multifamily portfolio signals continued debt availability for stabilized assets in supply-constrained sunbelt metros. Strong investor demand (multiple oversubscription) confirms ongoing appetite for Southwest rent-growth assets despite floating-rate risk; refinances of this size reduce refinance risk for operators and unlock capital for acquisitions/renovations in high-barrier Utah/Nevada markets.

stories.title: JLL Snares Listing for Legacy Central Office Campus
stories.excerpt: Three buildings totaling 706,395 square feet at Legacy Central in Plano have been listed for sale by JLL. The buildings are fully leased to a variety of blue-chip tenants, including Samsung Electronics, Nokia, Freddie Mac and Publicis. Samsung announced last month that it had chosen the offices to be its corporate US headquarters. The property has a weighted average lease term of 5.3 years. The Dallas Business Journal reports that Regent Properties and Hana Financial are the owners. Originally built in 1985 as Texas Instruments’ corporate headquarters, the campus underwent a $114 million renovation by Regent between 2016 and 2021. JLL’s Jonathan Napper, Macki McKim, Bailey Wood and Mike McDonald are marketing the property. No listing price has been disclosed. The deal comes as Dallas-Fort Worth remains the nation’s top metro for corporate headquarters relocations, according to CBRE. The post JLL Snares Listing for Legacy Central Office Campus appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Legacy Central Plano: 706,395 SF, three buildings, blue-chip tenants (Samsung, Nokia, Freddie Mac, Publicis).
Samsung selected as US HQ; weighted-average lease term 5.3 years; $114M renovation 2016–2021.
DFW remains nation's #1 metro for HQ relocations; original built 1985 as Texas Instruments HQ.
stories.summary: Regent Properties and Hana Financial have listed three buildings totaling 706,395 SF at Legacy Central in Plano for sale via JLL. The campus is fully leased to blue-chip tenants including Samsung Electronics (which recently named the offices its US headquarters), Nokia, Freddie Mac, and Publicis. The property has a 5.3-year weighted-average lease term and underwent a $114 million renovation between 2016–2021. Originally built as Texas Instruments' HQ in 1985.
stories.impact: Samsung's HQ selection at Legacy Central accelerates corporate-led migration into DFW, reinforcing the metro's position as a top HQ relocation hub and signaling continued job and wage-earning population inflow to North Dallas suburbs. This concentration of corporate anchors and office capital in Plano/Legacy submarket will drive ancillary multifamily demand (executive housing, workforce rental) in nearby submarkets; developers should monitor land availability within 3–5 miles of Legacy Central for workforce-focused multifamily targeting 1BR/2BR efficiency-to-mid-range units.

stories.title: Protective Live, Berkadia Provide $50M for Two Senior Living Facilities
stories.excerpt: Senior Living Transformation Company (SLTC) and Sabal Investment Holdings have secured $50 million to acquire and improve two senior living communities that specialize in assisted living and memory care: Daylesford Crossing in Paoli, Pa., and the Villages of Windcrest in Fredericksburg, Texas. Protective Life provided debt on the Villages of Windcrest, while Berkadia financed the Daylesford Crossing deal, according to a release. No broker was listed on the transaction. SLTC and Sabal plan numerous capital expenditures at the two assets, including improving the delivery of technology and operations, and will work with Juniper Communities, an established provider that will manage both facilities. “These acquisitions showcase SLTC’s and Sabal’s ability to provide solutions for challenged sellers within this critically important real estate sector,” said Arnie Whitman, founder and managing partner of SLTC. Located at 1450 East Lancaster Avenue in Paoli, a town 20 miles northwest of Downtown Philadelphia, Daylesford Crossing consists of 78 units. Located at 702 West Windcrest Street in Fredericksburg, a town 78 miles west of Austin, the Villages of Windcrest is 81 units. Tal Seder, managing director of Sabal Investment Holdings, described the two assets as “quality, well-located properties with upside potential” in a statement and referenced the demographic tailwinds from the baby boom generation that began turning 80 years old in 2026. “The combination of a sizable, aging baby boomer population and years of limited new construction is bringing the industry to an inflection point,” Seder said. “Investment in this sector is both critical and ripe with opportunity.” Brian Pascus can be reached at bpascus@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: SLTC and Sabal acquire two senior living facilities: Daylesford Crossing (Paoli, PA) and Villages of Windcrest (Fredericksburg, TX).
Protective Life and Berkadia provide $50M total; Juniper Communities to manage both; capital expenditure planned.
Sector focus on technology, operations improvement; acquisition of challenged assets by specialized operator.
stories.summary: Senior Living Transformation Company (SLTC) and Sabal Investment Holdings have acquired Daylesford Crossing (Paoli, PA, 20 miles northwest of Philadelphia) and The Villages of Windcrest (Fredericksburg, TX), two assisted living and memory care communities. Protective Life and Berkadia provided $50 million in financing. Juniper Communities will manage both properties. Operators plan significant capital expenditures in technology and operations.
stories.impact: Not materially relevant to multifamily development. Senior housing is a distinct asset class with different underwriting, labor, and regulatory profiles. However, if SLTC/Sabal's success signals consolidation of fragmented senior care operators, expect continued institutional capital redeployment toward specialized care operators over general multifamily, which may tighten capital competition in secondary markets (Fredericksburg, Paoli area) for workforce housing.

stories.title: Tishman Speyer, Breakthrough Properties Provide $90M Refi for Life Sciences Campus
stories.excerpt: The life sciences boom isn’t finished yet. Gemdale USA has secured $90 million in mezzanine debt to refinance Aperture Del Mar, a 538,000-square-foot Class A life science campus that recently opened in San Diego, Calif. Tishman Speyer and Breakthrough Properties, its life science joint venture vehicle with bellco capital, provided the loan, which will refinance existing debt. Breakthrough’s investment is financed out of a life sciences fund, which held its first close in late 2025. No broker was listed on the transaction. PERE was the first to report the news. Randall Rothschild, global head of debt at Tishman Speyer Global, noted that Breakthrough Properties already has “deep life science experience” in the marketplace, as the joint venture has financed several San Diego-area life sciences assets. He cited the San Diego region as being one of the epicenters for the ongoing growth of the asset class. “We are pleased to provide a creative financing solution that supports the continued advancement of a best-in-class life science project in one of the country’s premier innovation markets,” said Rothschild. Located at 6040 Edgewood Bend Court in San Diego, Aperture Del Mar finished its first phase of construction in 2021 and began leasing in 2023. The life sciences campus is divided among four lab buildings and a separate office space and is 100 percent occupied by Neurocrine Biosciences, a leading biopharmaceutical company that will call the site its global headquarters through 2036. Aside from its five different buildings, the campus includes a fitness center, a yoga studio, an outdoor lawn for events, a private courtyard, and 1,500-space parking garage. “Aperture Del Mar offers a true Class A campus environment, and Neurocrine, with more than three decades of history in San Diego, is one of the region’s marquee biotechnology companies,” said Dan D’Orazi, chief investment officer of Breakthrough Properties. bullets: Gemdale USA secures $90M mezzanine refi from Tishman Speyer/Breakthrough Properties for Aperture Del Mar (San Diego).
Aperture: 538,000 SF Class A life science campus; recently opened; Breakthrough Properties life science fund first close late 2025.

stories.summary: Gemdale USA has secured $90 million in mezzanine debt from Tishman Speyer and Breakthrough Properties (Tishman's life science JV with bellco capital) to refinance Aperture Del Mar, a newly opened 538,000 SF Class A life science campus in San Diego. Breakthrough Properties' life science fund reached first close in late 2025. The loan refinances existing debt on the recently delivered asset.

This may accelerate life science campus development and absorb capital, construction labor, and land in San Diego biotech corridors, indirectly raising hard costs and competing for skilled trades that could impact multifamily development timelines and budgets in the region.

stories.title: Nomura Prices Largest Single-Bank SASB CMBS in Two Years
stories.excerpt: As it approaches its first birthday, Nomura Securities’ commercial real estate lending platform has an extra reason to celebrate: It just sealed the largest sole-bank single-asset, single-borrower commercial mortgage-backed securities (SASB CMBS) deal in almost two years. The $719 million KELR 2026-MF deal is backed by 12 multifamily properties and one student housing asset, all owned by Keller Investment Properties. Nomura is the sole lender in the floating-rate, interest-only deal, which has a two-year term with three one-year extension options. The deal marks not only the largest single-bank SASB since August 2024, but it also places it among the largest single-bank SASB deals since 2020 — not too shabby for a platform that launched only last summer. Further, the transaction received a strong response from investors and was multiple times oversubscribed, sources said. Newmark brokered the financing, and the AAA bonds — rated by Fitch Ratings and Moody’s — priced at 135 basis points over the Secured Overnight Financing Rate earlier this week. The portfolio collateral is spread across Utah, Nevada and Arizona, and totals 3,321 units, including the sole student housing property in the portfolio, which accommodates students at Utah Valley University. Keller acquired the portfolio between 2001 and 2022, and has since invested $46 million in capital improvements, according to Fitch’s presale report. The CMBS loan proceeds will refinance $696 million in existing debt on the portfolio and also fund $22.2 million in closing-related costs and reserves. The transaction may have been a first for Nomura, but it was also one for Keller Investment Properties, based just outside of Salt Lake City, which historically has been a borrower of agency debt, sources said. As such, KELR 2026-MF marks the company’s SASB CMBS debut. bullets: Nomura prices $719M KELR 2026-MF SASB CMBS for Keller Investment Properties; 12 MF + 1 student housing asset.
Largest single-bank SASB since August 2024; floating-rate, interest-only, 2-year term with three 1-year extension options.
Deal oversubscribed; strong investor demand; Nomura CRE platform 1 year old; Newmark brokered.
stories.summary: Nomura Securities priced the $719 million KELR 2026-MF SASB CMBS, the largest sole-bank single-asset, single-borrower deal in nearly two years. Backed by Keller Investment Properties' 12 multifamily and 1 student housing asset, the floating-rate, interest-only, two-year loan includes three one-year extension options. The deal was oversubscribed; AAA bonds received strong investor pricing.
stories.impact: Nomura's successful solo-syndication of a large, oversubscribed multifamily SASB—less than one year after platform launch—signals robust institutional appetite for stabilized multifamily debt and confidence in floating-rate structures despite rate volatility. Large SASB capacity supports refinance liquidity for seasoned Southwest portfolios and lowers refi risk, enabling sponsors to redeploy equity into new development. This reinforces capital availability for quality assets in established markets (Utah, Nevada, Arizona).

stories.title: No, the Pfizer Near-Disaster Won’t Slow New York’s Conversion Wave
stories.excerpt: New York City is relying, in part, on more than 16,000 units planned via office-to-residential conversions to ease its enduring housing crisis. So, when the country’s largest conversion, sitting in the heart of Midtown, starts to buckle, it’s not taken lightly. The startling structural emergency at MetroLoft and David Werner Real Estate Investment’s Pfizer building conversion in early July prompted a swift response from the city. Reports of two buckling columns prompted officials to cordon off 40th to 45th streets between First and Third avenues in the immediate aftermath. Several buildings were evacuated, including a school where roughly 400 children were relocated. In the following weeks, after temporary supports secured the building, the New York City Department of Buildings (DOB) initiated citywide construction safety sweeps, including checks on projects linked to MetroLoft’s contractor, Barone Steel Fabricators, Gothamist reported. A full investigation of the emergency is ongoing, but the final verdict will likely come down to the two columns, and the heavy load above them. The real estate industry is largely in agreement that the Pfizer emergency was a freak accident. Yet, when a conversion of such fame and magnitude — in which 19 stories and 1,600 apartments are being added to the existing structure — causes such disruption, anxiety is understandable. New regulations from the city, and accompanying cost overruns, may now be the industry’s real worry. Is it enough to spook the market? Development, real estate and housing advocates sure hope not. Conversion projects, like any major development, experience pressures to stay on time and on budget, intensified by an inflationary, volatile capital markets environment and heightened construction costs in the Big Apple. Insiders argue that the scare is unlikely to derail New York’s office conversion boom, given the investor appetite and political will behind multifamily housing. bullets: MetroLoft/David Werner Real Estate's Pfizer building conversion (Midtown NYC) suffered structural buckling; 40–45 Sts evacuated.
NYC DoB initiated citywide construction safety sweeps linked to Barone Steel Fabricators contractor; full investigation ongoing.
NYC conversion pipeline: 16,000+ planned units; Pfizer building largest conversion; emergency does not slow wave.
stories.summary: The MetroLoft and David Werner Real Estate office-to-residential conversion of the Pfizer building in Midtown Manhattan experienced a structural emergency in July when two columns began buckling, prompting evacuation of blocks and relocation of ~400 schoolchildren. The NYC Department of Buildings launched citywide construction safety sweeps and is investigating contractor Barone Steel Fabricators. Despite this emergency, NYC's 16,000+-unit conversion pipeline—anchored by the Pfizer project—is not expected to slow.
stories.impact: The Pfizer structural failure and subsequent DoB crackdown create near-term uncertainty and potential delays for Midtown and citywide office conversion projects. Contractor liability, structural engineering remediation costs, and mandatory safety compliance will increase construction costs and extend timelines for ongoing conversions. However, NYC's severe housing shortage and the article's framing ("won't slow wave") suggest structural issues will be corrected without killing conversions; instead, expect tighter code enforcement, higher insurance/contingency budgets, and contractor consolidation toward larger, better-capitalized firms with proven structural expertise in Midtown conversion plays.
